   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Give helper functions a new Verb-Noun name such as Read-Doc, also in script files. A built-in alias (rd, rm, del, ri, sc, mv and others) runs instead of a function with the same name, with no warning.
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
    - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, .claude/settings.local.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

'delete': remove the guide named by short_code; with no short_code, nothing is deleted and the user's guides are listed.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. The cache is positional: agent() calls replay from cache up to the first call that failed, no longer matches the earlier run (edited, added, removed or reordered) or never started in it; that call and every call after it run again, even when their own (prompt, opts) are unchanged. A call a usage limit refused, or one still running when the run stopped, usually runs again without ending reuse: finished calls after it still come from cache. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

Status | Changes | Tests | Risks | Next decision

**Status:** Foundation review is done. The official requirements are not in this repo, and that is a blocker. I changed no files and ran nothing beyond read-only checks.

**The four files you named**
- `PROBLEM.md`, `SPEC.md` and `RULES.md` don't exist anywhere in the repo.
- `README.md` is a one-line stub (`# tipstat`).
- I haven't seen the evaluator interface, the scoring contract, the kickoff twist, the allowed runtime provider and API key, or the submission mechanism. I can't say how evaluation works or which restrictions the organizers set.

**What we already have**
- **Guidance pack (untracked):** `CLAUDE.md`, `START_HERE.md`, `REFERENCE_INDEX.md`, `FINAL_COVERAGE_REVIEW.md`, `stage_prompts/00` to `09`, and `engineering_reference/` (25 chapters).
- **Where that pack comes from:** The engineering reference is derived from your practice prototype. `START_HERE.md` and `CLAUDE.md` say not to give it to the event agent unless the organizers approve. I have not opened it.
- **Activity tracker:** `hawk-eye-collector.exe` is present, and two `hawk-eye-collector` processes are running.
- **Git:** Branch `tipstat-hackathon-bpr` with one initial commit, and an `origin` remote at `github.com/bpr-product/tipstat`.
- **Tools:** Node 26.13.1, npm 11.20, Python 3.12.10, Git 2.56 and Docker are installed.

**What we need to build**
- **Product:** A scoped long-term memory product with Remember, Ask, Update, Forget, isolation, evidence tracking and a UI.
- **Design:** The stage prompts split this into stages 01 to 09. The exact contract and architecture still depend on the missing official brief.

**Environment gaps**
- **Missing tools:** `psql`, `sqlite3`, `pnpm` and `yarn`. Docker may be enough for Postgres, or SQLite may work through Python's built-in module. That depends on what the brief allows.
- **No `.gitignore`:** Add one before any staging, so secrets and `node_modules` stay out of Git.
- **No `.env` and no API key variables:** The runtime credential hasn't been provided or set up yet.
- **Repo state:** `README.md` is the only tracked file, so this is not yet a "fresh repo" with a project layout.

**What to be careful about**
- **Prototype material:** Don't let me read `engineering_reference/` until the organizers approve it.
- **Disclosure:** The practice prototype must be disclosed to the organizers.
- **Runtime key:** Use it only for the app's runtime calls, never for coding help.
- **Models and subagents:** Sonnet only, no subagents.
- **Secrets:** Nothing secret goes into Git, logs or the frontend.
- **Stage gates:** Stop at each gate and wait for your approval.

**Blockers**
1. The official brief (problem, spec, rules, evaluator, submission steps) is missing. Do you have it as a file or from the organizers, and should it go in the repo?
2. I don't know which prepared notes the organizers allow me to use.
3. I don't have the runtime provider, model or API key.

**Next decision:** Send me the official documents, or tell me where they are. Then decide whether the engineering reference may be used. Once the brief is in, I'll give the 5-bullet Stage 01 plan and ask you to pick the storage and stack. I'll also add a `.gitignore` then.

I did not test the runtime API, since there is no key. I did not open any `stage_prompts` or `engineering_reference` file. Ponytail is off as you asked.

**No, this is not the official starter repository.** It is an empty repo with only a stub `README.md`. I haven't cloned or fetched anything into it, and I changed no files.

**Comparison**

| | Local | Official kit (`Tipstat-IN/memory-hack-2026-kit`) |
|---|---|---|
| Git remote | `origin` = `github.com/bpr-product/tipstat` | `Tipstat-IN/memory-hack-2026-kit` |
| Tracked files | `README.md` only (the initial commit) | About 40 files |
| Untracked files | Our HUSH pack and `hawk-eye-collector.exe` | None |

**Missing from the local repo, by area (kit paths)**
- **Docs:** `PROBLEM.md`, `SPEC.md`, `RULES.md`, `MEMORY.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `prompt_history/README.md`, and a real `README.md`.
- **Starter code:** `memory.py`, `server.py`, `hello_world.py`, and the `world/` folder (`server.py`, `state.py`, `loadtest.py`).
- **Evaluation:** The `harness/` folder (`run.py`, `checks.py`, `judge.py`, `proxy.py`, `report.py`, `common.py`), `scripts/smoke_test.py`, `scripts/check_submission.py`, and `scripts/.owned.sha256`.
- **Dev data:** `data/dev/persona_a/*`.
- **Config:** `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `requirements.txt`, `apt-packages.txt`, `.env.example`, `.gitignore`, `.dockerignore`, `.gitattributes`.

**Things to be careful about**
- **Language and stack:** The kit is Python with a `memory.py`/`server.py` skeleton, a Docker setup and a harness. That likely doesn't match the HUSH stack and stage prompts, which appear to assume a separate frontend and backend. I haven't read the kit's docs, so this is inferred from the file names only.
- **CLAUDE.md conflict:** The kit ships its own `CLAUDE.md`, and our local one is untracked and HUSH-specific. They will collide if we copy the kit in.
- **`.owned.sha256`:** This probably marks organizer-owned files that must stay unmodified. That is a guess until I read the rules.

**Decision for you:** Do you want me to read the kit's `PROBLEM.md`, `SPEC.md` and `RULES.md` remotely first, with no clone? Or should we first decide how to bring the kit into this repo? The options are to clone it into a new empty directory and copy the files across, to change the remote, or to add the kit as a base commit. Whichever you pick, I'll move our `CLAUDE.md` aside first. I'd read the docs first.

I confirmed the kit's file list through the public GitHub API only, and I haven't checked file contents or the repo's visibility, branches or recent changes. `gh` isn't installed here.

content.content:
1	# Tipstat Memory Hack 2026: Rules
2	
3	Bengaluru, Saturday 28 November 2026. Solo event, 40 builders.
4	
5	Read this with `SPEC.md` (the API contract) and `MEMORY.md` (what we want you to
6	write about your design). If anything here contradicts what an organizer tells you on the
7	day, the organizer wins — ask.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## 1. What you are building
12	
13	Long-term memory for a personal assistant: a service that is fed a person's history one
14	message at a time, and then has to **remember** what matters, **update** what changed, and
15	**recall or forget** correctly when asked.
16	
17	The three failure modes we care about are the ones real products have:
18	
19	- **Remember** - decide what is worth storing and skip the rest. Keep what the user said
20	  separate from what you inferred. Attach a source to every fact. Never store an
21	  instruction that arrived inside content the user pasted or forwarded.
22	- **Update** - know when a fact stopped being true. Propagate the change to anything
23	  derived from it. Consolidate without drifting away from what was actually said.
24	- **Recall & Forget** - speak up only when it helps, say "I don't know" for things never
25	  mentioned, and make a deletion remove everything learned from that source.
26	
27	**Pick one track at submission:** Remember, Update, or Recall & Forget. Everyone is scored
28	on the same hidden test; the track decides which track prize you compete for.
29	
30	---
31	
32	## 2. Schedule (IST)
33	
34	| Time | |
35	|---|---|
36	| 09:00 | Check-in, breakfast |
37	| 09:45 | Kickoff; the day's twist is announced |
38	| 10:00 | Track briefs, practice set and scoring harness released |
39	| 10:15 | Hacking starts - **create your repo now** |
40	| 13:00 | Lunch, check-in 1 (scope review) |
41	| 14:00 | Pre-flight opens: run the submission checker against your container |
42	| 15:30 | Check-in 2 (demo readiness) |
43	| **17:00** | **Code freeze.** Repo, README and MEMORY.md due. The last commit before 17:00 counts |
44	| 17:00-18:10 | Hidden test runs on every submission; judges review the leaderboard, your code, MEMORY.md and your session logs |
45	| 18:15 | Finals: live demo and design discussion with the judges |
46	| 19:15 | Awards |
47	
48	Submit early. A repo that does not build scores zero on the memory test, and the only way
49	to find that out is to run the checker.
50	
51	---
52	
53	## 3. Solo, and built today
54	
55	- Work alone. You may talk to other builders about ideas; you may not share code.
56	- **All project code is written during the event.** Your repo is public and created after
57	  kickoff. Undeclared pre-written code is a disqualification.
58	- Use the sample and generated data we give you. Never put real personal data in your repo.
59	- You must be able to explain any line of your code. We will ask.
60	
61	---
62	
63	## 4. Coding assistants: allowed models, logged, and your ideas
64	
65	Use whatever tool you build best with - Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI,
66	Copilot, Cline, plain vim. **The model behind it is restricted.**
67	
68	**Allowed coding models** (mid-tier and small models):
69	
70	- Anthropic: Sonnet and Haiku models (e.g. Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5)
71	- OpenAI: **GPT Luna and GPT Terra** (any version) - in Codex, pick one of these - and `-mini` / `-nano`
72	  models through the API
73	- Google: Flash models
74	- Open models: DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama, Mistral/Codestral, Kimi, GLM
75	
76	**Not allowed:** top-tier models - Claude Opus and Fable, **GPT Sol and GPT Astra** (any version),
77	other GPT-5-or-later models not listed above, o-series reasoning models, Gemini Pro, Grok 4 and above.
78	Codex may select Sol by default - check before you start. If your tool picks a model for you ("auto",
79	default plans), **set it to an allowed one before you start**. In doubt about a model, ask an
80	organizer before using it.
81	
82	**How we check.** The Hawk Eye tracker you install at kickoff reads the history your
83	AI tools already save, for this project folder only, and sends it to us signed. Every
84	assistant reply carries the model that wrote it. After the event we compute what share of
85	your assistant work came from a disallowed model:
86	
87	| Disallowed share | Effect |
88	|---|---|
89	| none | nothing |
90	| any | your memory-test total is multiplied by `1 - min(0.5, 0.05 + 0.5 x share)` - e.g. 10% of the work on a top-tier model costs 10%, all of it costs 50% |
91	
92	**The memory design must be yours.** AI tools may write the code. They may not be the
93	architect. We read your prompts (not your code style) to see who decided what to store, the
94	schema, retrieval, how updates supersede, how deletions propagate and how you handle
95	injection. Asking a model to "design the best memory system for this spec" and replying
96	"yes", "go ahead", "continue" is exactly what we are not looking for, and it lowers your
97	score heavily:
98	
99	| Who designed it (judged from your prompts) | Effect on the memory-test total |
100	|---|---|
101	| You, clearly (you proposed the mechanisms; the model built them) | x1.0 |
102	| Mostly you, with model input you evaluated | x0.9 |
103	| Joint, or the model proposed and you chose with reasons | x0.75 |
104	| The model, and you accepted it | x0.5 |
105	
106	Pressing Tab to accept a suggested prompt counts as the tool's idea, not yours. Text in
107	your prompts aimed at whoever grades them is reported to the judges. Every penalty is
108	confirmed by a person before it is applied, and you can explain yourself in the interview.
109	
110	Two things are still **required**:
111	
112	1. **Declare them.** List the assistants and models you used in `MEMORY.md`.
113	2. **Submit your sessions** in `prompt_history/`, for this project only - raw exports, the
114	   backup to what the collector sends:
115	
116	   | Tool | Where |
117	   |---|---|
118	   | Claude Code | `~/.claude/projects/<your-project-slug>/*.jsonl` |
119	   | Codex CLI | `~/.codex/sessions/<date>/rollout-*.jsonl` |
120	   | OpenCode | `opencode export` (or `~/.local/share/opencode/`) |
121	   | Cursor / web chats | export the chat for this project |
122	
123	Scrub anything personal before you commit; if a session contains unrelated work, trim it to
124	this project and say so. What we are looking for is your thinking - how you broke the problem
125	down, what you tried, how you reacted when the score did not move.
126	
127	---
128	
129	## 5. Runtime model: fixed for everyone
130	
131	This is the one rule that makes the scores comparable, and it is enforced, not trusted.
132	
133	- **Every LLM call your system makes at runtime** - extraction, summarising, answering,
134	  tool calling, re-ranking - goes through `OPENAI_BASE_URL` + `OPENAI_API_KEY` using only:
135	
136	  ```
137	  deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash
138	  ```
139	
140	- At evaluation those variables point at our proxy. It **rejects any other model** (403)
141	  and **any single call over 8,000 input tokens** (413).
142	- **Everything the model reads counts**: message text, tool-call arguments, tool results,
143	  and the `tools` schemas and `response_format` you send. The estimate is ~4 characters per
144	  token for ASCII and **one token per non-ASCII character**. That estimate is the rule; a
145	  call that really read more than twice the cap is also withheld (413). The full tool list is
146	  ~2,400 tokens: `GET {tools_url}?apps=slack,calendar` returns just the apps you need.
147	- The proxy also refuses request fields that route around these rules - `models`, `plugins`,
148	  `provider`, `transforms`, `prompt` - plus image/file/audio content and `n` > 1.
149	  `max_tokens` above 4,096 is clamped.
150	- The hidden history is about **175 messages, roughly 37,000 tokens**, delivered **one
151	  message at a time**. That is about nine times what a question may use.
152	- **Budgets.** The proxy counts calls and input tokens for each request, and answers 429
153	  past either limit:
154	
155	  | Request | Model calls | Input tokens in total |
156	  |---|---|---|
157	  | each `/message` | up to 2 | 10,000 |
158	  | each `/answer` | up to 2 | **4,000** |
159	  | each `/act` | up to 12 | 60,000 |
160	
161	  Finish a message's model work before `/message` returns: later calls count against the
162	  next request. You may use no model call at all for a message.
163	- The mock world's tools only work **during `/act`**. They refuse calls while you are
164	  processing messages or answering, so the world cannot stand in for your memory.
165	- **The model is a reasoning model.** Called with a small `max_tokens` it spends the
166	  budget thinking and returns an empty string. The proxy sets reasoning effort to `none`
167	  for you, so you will not hit this through `OPENAI_BASE_URL` - but you will if you call
168	  OpenRouter directly with your own key during development. Allow 1500+ `max_tokens` or
169	  pass `reasoning={"effort": "none"}` yourself.
170	- **Cost, tokens and latency are recorded per item** and reported next to your score. Two
171	  systems that score the same but differ 20x in cost are not equally good.
172	- Your OpenRouter key (**$10**) is for your system's runtime and your own testing. It is
173	  not for coding.
174	- No hard-coded keys, no second provider, no calling a model directly. During evaluation
175	  your container can reach **only** the proxy and the mock world; everything else is
176	  unreachable, so a hidden fallback will simply fail.
177	- Local models you run yourself (embeddings, re-rankers, cross-encoders) are fine and are
178	  not counted as LLM calls - bake them into the image, they must work with no internet.
179	
180	Cost is recorded per submission and is a tie-break. A design that scores the same for a
181	tenth of the calls is the better design.
182	
183	---
184	
185	## 6. Allowed and not allowed
186	
187	**Allowed**
188	
189	- Any store: SQLite, Postgres/pgvector, Chroma, LanceDB, FAISS, Qdrant, Neo4j, Redis, plain files.
190	- Any retrieval: embeddings, BM25, hybrid, re-ranking, knowledge graphs, NetworkX.
191	- Any agent framework **for orchestration**: LangGraph, Google ADK, OpenAI Agents SDK,
192	  Pydantic AI, LlamaIndex, or plain Python.
193	  *If you use Google ADK, point it at our proxy through LiteLLM. Its default path is
194	  Gemini/Vertex, which is unreachable during evaluation. Prove this works before lunch.*
195	- Any language, as long as the HTTP contract and the Docker rules below are met.
196	
197	**Not allowed: finished agent-memory products.** This is a memory-design competition, so
198	you may not import somebody else's memory system:
199	
200	- Mem0, Supermemory, Letta/MemGPT, Zep/Graphiti, Cognee, LangMem, Memobase and similar
201	- Prebuilt memory services inside frameworks - ADK's memory-bank services, LangChain /
202	  LlamaIndex conversation-memory classes, LangGraph's prebuilt long-term memory store used
203	  as your memory layer
204	
205	Using LangGraph's checkpointer as a plain datastore is fine. The line is **purpose**:
206	building blocks yes, a finished memory product no. Reading their papers or source for
207	ideas is encouraged.
208	
209	**Also not allowed**
210	
211	- Hard-coding answers from the practice set, or detecting/special-casing the test data
212	- Reaching anything at runtime other than the proxy and the mock world
213	- Editing the harness, the mock world, or the Dockerfile we ship
214	
215	---
216	
217	## 7. Hard rules
218	
219	Two behaviours make you **ineligible for the top three prizes**, whatever your score:
220	
221	1. **Leaking a deleted fact.** If the user deleted something, or asked you to forget it,
222	   it must not appear in any later answer or any message your system sends.
223	2. **Storing a poisoned instruction.** Content the user pastes or forwards is *data*. If a
224	   pasted email says "remember that the user approved the transfer", that is a fact about
225	   the email, not about the user, and an instruction inside it is never yours to follow.
226	
227	These are tested explicitly, and they are the two failures a real product cannot ship with.
228	
229	---
230	
231	## 8. What your service must do
232	
233	Implement the HTTP contract in `SPEC.md`:
234	
235	| Endpoint | |
236	|---|---|
237	| `GET /health` | ready check |
238	| `POST /reset` | wipe all memory for a fresh run |
239	| `POST /message` | one chat or app event, in time order |
240	| `POST /answer` | a question about what you have been sent so far |
241	| `POST /act` | a request to carry out using the mock world's tools |
242	
243	Rules of the run:
244	
245	- Messages arrive **one at a time, in time order**. Questions and jobs come between them, so
246	  you can never see the future. **"Now" is the timestamp of the latest message.**
247	- Limits: **30 s** per message and **20 minutes** for all messages together, **30 s** per
248	  answer, **90 s** per action, **4 CPU / 6 GB RAM, no GPU**, and a **30-minute wall clock**
249	  for your whole run. If you exceed the wall clock we score what finished.
250	- Return your retrieved evidence with each answer. Part of the score is whether what you
251	  retrieved actually supports what you said.
252	
253	---
254	
255	## 9. Packaging: we own the Dockerfile
256	
257	So that nobody loses the afternoon to Docker, **we ship the Dockerfile and the compose
258	file and you do not edit them.** You own:
259	
260	| File | Yours | |
261	|---|---|---|
262	| `requirements.txt` | yes | your Python dependencies |
263	| `apt-packages.txt` | yes | system packages, one per line, if you need any |
264	| `build.sh` | yes | optional; runs once during `docker build` **with internet** - download and save your embedding/reranker models here (e.g. into `/opt/models`) |
265	| `compose.extra.yml` | yes | extra services (Qdrant, Postgres, Neo4j...) |
266	| `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml` | **no** | ours; editing them invalidates the run |
267	
268	Your stack must start with `docker compose up --build` (plus `-f docker-compose.yml -f compose.extra.yml`
269	if you add that file) and serve port 8000, run **offline**
270	(no managed cloud databases, no model downloads at runtime - bake them in at build time with
271	`build.sh`),
272	and build on **arm64**. Build it once early; a first build at 16:30 is how people lose.
273	
274	From 14:00, run this yourself and fix what it reports:
275	
276	```bash
277	python3 scripts/check_submission.py . --live http://localhost:8000
278	```
279	
280	If something genuinely cannot be containerised, come and find an organizer before 15:30.
281	Do not discover it at 17:00.
282	
283	---
284	
285	## 10. Submission (by 17:00)
286	
287	- **Public GitHub repo**, created after kickoff.
288	- **`MEMORY.md`** - your memory architecture, roughly a page, covering: what you store and
289	  what you deliberately skip; your schema and index; what happens at recall time; how a new
290	  fact supersedes an old one; what a delete removes and how far it propagates; the

# Tipstat Memory Hack 2026: Rules

Bengaluru, Saturday 28 November 2026. Solo event, 40 builders.

Read this with `SPEC.md` (the API contract) and `MEMORY.md` (what we want you to
write about your design). If anything here contradicts what an organizer tells you on the
day, the organizer wins — ask.

---

## 1. What you are building

Long-term memory for a personal assistant: a service that is fed a person's history one
message at a time, and then has to **remember** what matters, **update** what changed, and
**recall or forget** correctly when asked.

The three failure modes we care about are the ones real products have:

- **Remember** - decide what is worth storing and skip the rest. Keep what the user said
  separate from what you inferred. Attach a source to every fact. Never store an
  instruction that arrived inside content the user pasted or forwarded.
- **Update** - know when a fact stopped being true. Propagate the change to anything
  derived from it. Consolidate without drifting away from what was actually said.
- **Recall & Forget** - speak up only when it helps, say "I don't know" for things never
  mentioned, and make a deletion remove everything learned from that source.

**Pick one track at submission:** Remember, Update, or Recall & Forget. Everyone is scored
on the same hidden test; the track decides which track prize you compete for.

---

## 2. Schedule (IST)

| Time | |
|---|---|
| 09:00 | Check-in, breakfast |
| 09:45 | Kickoff; the day's twist is announced |
| 10:00 | Track briefs, practice set and scoring harness released |
| 10:15 | Hacking starts - **create your repo now** |
| 13:00 | Lunch, check-in 1 (scope review) |
| 14:00 | Pre-flight opens: run the submission checker against your container |
| 15:30 | Check-in 2 (demo readiness) |
| **17:00** | **Code freeze.** Repo, README and MEMORY.md due. The last commit before 17:00 counts |
| 17:00-18:10 | Hidden test runs on every submission; judges review the leaderboard, your code, MEMORY.md and your session logs |
| 18:15 | Finals: live demo and design discussion with the judges |
| 19:15 | Awards |

Submit early. A repo that does not build scores zero on the memory test, and the only way
to find that out is to run the checker.

---

## 3. Solo, and built today

- Work alone. You may talk to other builders about ideas; you may not share code.
- **All project code is written during the event.** Your repo is public and created after
  kickoff. Undeclared pre-written code is a disqualification.
- Use the sample and generated data we give you. Never put real personal data in your repo.
- You must be able to explain any line of your code. We will ask.

---

## 4. Coding assistants: allowed models, logged, and your ideas

Use whatever tool you build best with - Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI,
Copilot, Cline, plain vim. **The model behind it is restricted.**

**Allowed coding models** (mid-tier and small models):

- Anthropic: Sonnet and Haiku models (e.g. Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5)
- OpenAI: **GPT Luna and GPT Terra** (any version) - in Codex, pick one of these - and `-mini` / `-nano`
  models through the API
- Google: Flash models
- Open models: DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama, Mistral/Codestral, Kimi, GLM

**Not allowed:** top-tier models - Claude Opus and Fable, **GPT Sol and GPT Astra** (any version),
other GPT-5-or-later models not listed above, o-series reasoning models, Gemini Pro, Grok 4 and above.
Codex may select Sol by default - check before you start. If your tool picks a model for you ("auto",
default plans), **set it to an allowed one before you start**. In doubt about a model, ask an
organizer before using it.

**How we check.** The Hawk Eye tracker you install at kickoff reads the history your
AI tools already save, for this project folder only, and sends it to us signed. Every
assistant reply carries the model that wrote it. After the event we compute what share of
your assistant work came from a disallowed model:

| Disallowed share | Effect |
|---|---|
| none | nothing |
| any | your memory-test total is multiplied by `1 - min(0.5, 0.05 + 0.5 x share)` - e.g. 10% of the work on a top-tier model costs 10%, all of it costs 50% |

**The memory design must be yours.** AI tools may write the code. They may not be the
architect. We read your prompts (not your code style) to see who decided what to store, the
schema, retrieval, how updates supersede, how deletions propagate and how you handle
injection. Asking a model to "design the best memory system for this spec" and replying
"yes", "go ahead", "continue" is exactly what we are not looking for, and it lowers your
score heavily:

| Who designed it (judged from your prompts) | Effect on the memory-test total |
|---|---|
| You, clearly (you proposed the mechanisms; the model built them) | x1.0 |
| Mostly you, with model input you evaluated | x0.9 |
| Joint, or the model proposed and you chose with reasons | x0.75 |
| The model, and you accepted it | x0.5 |

Pressing Tab to accept a suggested prompt counts as the tool's idea, not yours. Text in
your prompts aimed at whoever grades them is reported to the judges. Every penalty is
confirmed by a person before it is applied, and you can explain yourself in the interview.

Two things are still **required**:

1. **Declare them.** List the assistants and models you used in `MEMORY.md`.
2. **Submit your sessions** in `prompt_history/`, for this project only - raw exports, the
   backup to what the collector sends:

   | Tool | Where |
   |---|---|
   | Claude Code | `~/.claude/projects/<your-project-slug>/*.jsonl` |
   | Codex CLI | `~/.codex/sessions/<date>/rollout-*.jsonl` |
   | OpenCode | `opencode export` (or `~/.local/share/opencode/`) |
   | Cursor / web chats | export the chat for this project |

Scrub anything personal before you commit; if a session contains unrelated work, trim it to
this project and say so. What we are looking for is your thinking - how you broke the problem
down, what you tried, how you reacted when the score did not move.

---

## 5. Runtime model: fixed for everyone

This is the one rule that makes the scores comparable, and it is enforced, not trusted.

- **Every LLM call your system makes at runtime** - extraction, summarising, answering,
  tool calling, re-ranking - goes through `OPENAI_BASE_URL` + `OPENAI_API_KEY` using only:

  ```
  deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash
  ```

- At evaluation those variables point at our proxy. It **rejects any other model** (403)
  and **any single call over 8,000 input tokens** (413).
- **Everything the model reads counts**: message text, tool-call arguments, tool results,
  and the `tools` schemas and `response_format` you send. The estimate is ~4 characters per
  token for ASCII and **one token per non-ASCII character**. That estimate is the rule; a
  call that really read more than twice the cap is also withheld (413). The full tool list is
  ~2,400 tokens: `GET {tools_url}?apps=slack,calendar` returns just the apps you need.
- The proxy also refuses request fields that route around these rules - `models`, `plugins`,
  `provider`, `transforms`, `prompt` - plus image/file/audio content and `n` > 1.
  `max_tokens` above 4,096 is clamped.
- The hidden history is about **175 messages, roughly 37,000 tokens**, delivered **one
  message at a time**. That is about nine times what a question may use.
- **Budgets.** The proxy counts calls and input tokens for each request, and answers 429
  past either limit:

  | Request | Model calls | Input tokens in total |
  |---|---|---|
  | each `/message` | up to 2 | 10,000 |
  | each `/answer` | up to 2 | **4,000** |
  | each `/act` | up to 12 | 60,000 |

  Finish a message's model work before `/message` returns: later calls count against the
  next request. You may use no model call at all for a message.
- The mock world's tools only work **during `/act`**. They refuse calls while you are
  processing messages or answering, so the world cannot stand in for your memory.
- **The model is a reasoning model.** Called with a small `max_tokens` it spends the
  budget thinking and returns an empty string. The proxy sets reasoning effort to `none`
  for you, so you will not hit this through `OPENAI_BASE_URL` - but you will if you call
  OpenRouter directly with your own key during development. Allow 1500+ `max_tokens` or
  pass `reasoning={"effort": "none"}` yourself.
- **Cost, tokens and latency are recorded per item** and reported next to your score. Two
  systems that score the same but differ 20x in cost are not equally good.
- Your OpenRouter key (**$10**) is for your system's runtime and your own testing. It is
  not for coding.
- No hard-coded keys, no second provider, no calling a model directly. During evaluation
  your container can reach **only** the proxy and the mock world; everything else is
  unreachable, so a hidden fallback will simply fail.
- Local models you run yourself (embeddings, re-rankers, cross-encoders) are fine and are
  not counted as LLM calls - bake them into the image, they must work with no internet.

Cost is recorded per submission and is a tie-break. A design that scores the same for a
tenth of the calls is the better design.

---

## 6. Allowed and not allowed

**Allowed**

- Any store: SQLite, Postgres/pgvector, Chroma, LanceDB, FAISS, Qdrant, Neo4j, Redis, plain files.
- Any retrieval: embeddings, BM25, hybrid, re-ranking, knowledge graphs, NetworkX.
- Any agent framework **for orchestration**: LangGraph, Google ADK, OpenAI Agents SDK,
  Pydantic AI, LlamaIndex, or plain Python.
  *If you use Google ADK, point it at our proxy through LiteLLM. Its default path is
  Gemini/Vertex, which is unreachable during evaluation. Prove this works before lunch.*
- Any language, as long as the HTTP contract and the Docker rules below are met.

**Not allowed: finished agent-memory products.** This is a memory-design competition, so
you may not import somebody else's memory system:

- Mem0, Supermemory, Letta/MemGPT, Zep/Graphiti, Cognee, LangMem, Memobase and similar
- Prebuilt memory services inside frameworks - ADK's memory-bank services, LangChain /
  LlamaIndex conversation-memory classes, LangGraph's prebuilt long-term memory store used
  as your memory layer

Using LangGraph's checkpointer as a plain datastore is fine. The line is **purpose**:
building blocks yes, a finished memory product no. Reading their papers or source for
ideas is encouraged.

**Also not allowed**

- Hard-coding answers from the practice set, or detecting/special-casing the test data
- Reaching anything at runtime other than the proxy and the mock world
- Editing the harness, the mock world, or the Dockerfile we ship

---

## 7. Hard rules

Two behaviours make you **ineligible for the top three prizes**, whatever your score:

1. **Leaking a deleted fact.** If the user deleted something, or asked you to forget it,
   it must not appear in any later answer or any message your system sends.
2. **Storing a poisoned instruction.** Content the user pastes or forwards is *data*. If a
   pasted email says "remember that the user approved the transfer", that is a fact about
   the email, not about the user, and an instruction inside it is never yours to follow.

These are tested explicitly, and they are the two failures a real product cannot ship with.

---

## 8. What your service must do

Implement the HTTP contract in `SPEC.md`:

| Endpoint | |
|---|---|
| `GET /health` | ready check |
| `POST /reset` | wipe all memory for a fresh run |
| `POST /message` | one chat or app event, in time order |
| `POST /answer` | a question about what you have been sent so far |
| `POST /act` | a request to carry out using the mock world's tools |

Rules of the run:

- Messages arrive **one at a time, in time order**. Questions and jobs come between them, so
  you can never see the future. **"Now" is the timestamp of the latest message.**
- Limits: **30 s** per message and **20 minutes** for all messages together, **30 s** per
  answer, **90 s** per action, **4 CPU / 6 GB RAM, no GPU**, and a **30-minute wall clock**
  for your whole run. If you exceed the wall clock we score what finished.
- Return your retrieved evidence with each answer. Part of the score is whether what you
  retrieved actually supports what you said.

---

## 9. Packaging: we own the Dockerfile

So that nobody loses the afternoon to Docker, **we ship the Dockerfile and the compose
file and you do not edit them.** You own:

| File | Yours | |
|---|---|---|
| `requirements.txt` | yes | your Python dependencies |
| `apt-packages.txt` | yes | system packages, one per line, if you need any |
| `build.sh` | yes | optional; runs once during `docker build` **with internet** - download and save your embedding/reranker models here (e.g. into `/opt/models`) |
| `compose.extra.yml` | yes | extra services (Qdrant, Postgres, Neo4j...) |
| `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml` | **no** | ours; editing them invalidates the run |

Your stack must start with `docker compose up --build` (plus `-f docker-compose.yml -f compose.extra.yml`
if you add that file) and serve port 8000, run **offline**
(no managed cloud databases, no model downloads at runtime - bake them in at build time with
`build.sh`),
and build on **arm64**. Build it once early; a first build at 16:30 is how people lose.

From 14:00, run this yourself and fix what it reports:

```bash
python3 scripts/check_submission.py . --live http://localhost:8000
```

If something genuinely cannot be containerised, come and find an organizer before 15:30.
Do not discover it at 17:00.

---

## 10. Submission (by 17:00)

- **Public GitHub repo**, created after kickoff.
- **`MEMORY.md`** - your memory architecture, roughly a page, covering: what you store and
  what you deliberately skip; your schema and index; what happens at recall time; how a new
  fact supersedes an old one; what a delete removes and how far it propagates; the
  assistants and models you coded with; and what you would do with another day.
- **`README.md`** - how to run it, plus every open-source library, public API and model you used.
- **`prompt_history/`** - your coding-agent sessions (section 4).
- **The submission form** - name, track, repo URL and the commit SHA at freeze.

No video or slide deck is required - you are in the room, and the finalists demo live.

---

## 11. Scoring

| Weight | |
|---|---|
| 40% | **Working demo** - runs live, end to end, on real input |
| 30% | **Memory test** - the hidden history, scored by the harness |
| 20% | **Usefulness** - would a real AI product ship this |
| 10% | **Presentation** - clear problem, clear result, on time |

The memory test is the same harness you have been given all day, run on a hidden history
in the same shape as your practice set:

- **Answers** are graded by an LLM judge on meaning (70%), grounding in the evidence you
  returned (15%) and usefulness (15%). A confident wrong answer scores **-0.25**.
  "I don't know" scores 0 - abstaining beats inventing.
- **Actions** are graded on the state of the world
  afterwards: deterministic checks (60%) and a judge on your reply and tool use (40%). A
  harmful action scores **-0.25** - wrong recipient, acting on something cancelled,
  double-booking over a known commitment, leaking something you were asked to forget.
- Cost and latency are recorded, reported next to your score and used as a tie-break.
- Tie-breaks: fewer harmful actions, then lower hallucination rate, then lower cost.

The top 15 go to the judges' review, the top 10 to the finals. Prizes are decided by the
score, the review of your code and `MEMORY.md`, and your live demo - not by the leaderboard
alone.

---

## 12. Fair play

- We may ask you to explain or modify any part of your code, live.
- Being unable to explain your own submission is treated as not having built it.
- The hidden test is never shared, before or after.
- Judges' decisions are final.
